title: Insurance Services
summary: Risk is the possibility of loss or damage due to factors over which the businessman has little or no control. By cause, risks are natural (earthquake, flood, lightning), human (theft, dishonesty of employees or customers, strikes and lockouts, negligence) and economic (changes in fashion, demand, prices, competition, government policy). By type: pure risk (only loss or no loss — fire, theft); speculative risk (chance of both gain and loss — change in fashion or price); property risk; personnel risk (illness or death of employees); financial risk (from borrowing or investment decisions); marketing risk.

Insurance is a contract by which the risk of loss is shifted to another party, the insurer (insurance company or underwriter), in return for a payment called the premium; the person insured is the insured. The written contract is the policy. Insurance spreads the loss of a few over many. Importance: gives security and peace of mind; compensates business losses and so keeps firms running; helps large-scale production and trade; makes loans easier (policies serve as security); encourages saving and provides funds for national investment; generates employment; provides social security — so insurance is also a social service.

Life insurance (life assurance): the insurer pays a fixed sum on the death of the insured or at the end of a fixed period — the event is certain, only its timing is uncertain, so it is not a contract of indemnity. Whole-life policy: premium paid all life, sum paid to heirs after death. Endowment policy: runs for a fixed period; sum paid at maturity or on earlier death. Group insurance covers employees.

Fire insurance: compensates loss or damage by accidental fire, normally for one year (maximum). It is a contract of indemnity — the claim is the actual loss or the sum insured, whichever is less (policy ₹20,000, loss ₹15,000 → claim ₹15,000).

Marine insurance: covers perils of the sea — cargo insurance (goods), hull insurance (the ship) and freight insurance (the freight earned). Policies: time policy (a fixed period, usually one year); voyage policy (a particular voyage, whatever time it takes); mixed policy (a voyage within a time); floating policy (a round sum reduced as shipments are declared). Other general insurance: motor vehicle, burglary, fidelity (against dishonesty of employees), health, crop and liability insurance. Life insurance is not general insurance.

(1) Utmost good faith — both parties must disclose all material facts; hiding a disease or the use of explosive chemicals makes the contract void. (2) Insurable interest — the insured must stand to lose financially from the loss: in life insurance at the time of taking the policy (a divorce later does not affect a policy on a wife's life); in marine at the time of loss; in fire at both times. A mortgagee can insure the mortgaged property. (3) Indemnity — the insured is put back in his position before the loss and cannot profit from insurance; applies to fire and marine, not life. (4) Contribution — if the same property is insured with several insurers, they share the loss in proportion to their policies, and the insured cannot recover more than the loss. (5) Subrogation — after paying the claim, the insurer takes over the insured's rights in the damaged property (half-burnt goods belong to the insurer). (6) Mitigation — the insured must take all reasonable steps to reduce the loss. (7) Causa proxima — the insurer pays only if the nearest cause of loss is the risk insured against (oranges spoilt by delay in unloading are not covered by an accident policy).

objective: A Mumbai company shipping textiles to Dubai buys an insurance policy valid only for this particular trip, regardless of the time taken. (a) Identify the type of marine policy. (b) For what kind of insurance is it mostly used?

(a) Voyage policy.
(b) Cargo insurance.

Match the risks: (a) Pure risk (b) Financial risk — (i) arises from borrowing or investment decisions (ii) involves only the possibility of loss or no loss (iii) involves both gain and loss.

(a) Pure risk — (ii) only loss or no loss.
(b) Financial risk — (i) borrowing or investment decisions.
(Speculative risk involves both gain and loss; personnel risk arises from illness or death of employees.)

vsa: After the insurer has paid the claim, it steps into the shoes of the insured and gets all his rights in the damaged property. For example, if goods are partly destroyed by fire and the claim is paid, the insurer can take and sell the salvage. It prevents the insured from making a profit.
Distinguish between a whole-life policy and an endowment policy.

Whole-life: runs for the insured's whole life; premium is paid throughout; the sum is paid to the heirs only after death.
Endowment: runs for a fixed period or up to a certain age; the sum is paid at maturity, or to the heirs if the insured dies earlier.
What is insurance? Why is it called a social service?

Insurance is a contract by which the insurer agrees, for a premium, to compensate the insured for a specified loss. It is a social service because it spreads the loss of a few among many, gives security to families and businesses, and its funds are used for national development.
sa: Why is insurance considered important? State any three reasons.

(1) Security — it removes worry by compensating losses from fire, accidents and death.
(2) Helps business — firms can recover losses and continue; policies also serve as security for loans.
(3) Encourages saving and capital formation — premiums are invested in industry and government securities.
(Also: helps trade, provides employment and social security.)

Banita, Promil and Veena insured their godown for ₹10 lakh. A fire destroyed goods worth ₹6 lakh, which the insurer paid. They then sold the half-burnt goods for ₹50,000. Who should get this amount? Explain the principle.

The insurance company. By the principle of subrogation, after paying the claim the insurer gets all the rights of the insured in the damaged goods; otherwise the firm would get more than its loss, against the principle of indemnity.

or: Aman took a ₹25 lakh fire policy but hid the use of highly explosive chemicals to avoid a higher premium. After a fire the insurer refused the claim. Can Aman claim? Which principle was violated?
No, Aman cannot claim. He violated the principle of utmost good faith — he did not disclose a material fact (the explosive chemicals) that affects the risk and the premium, so the contract is void.

sa: Ajay's business suffers from changes in fashion and prices and tough competition; Vijay's from dishonesty of employees and customers and from strikes. Name the types of business risk.

Ajay — economic-cause risks (changes in fashion, prices, competition; speculative risks).
Vijay — human-cause risks (dishonesty of employees and customers, strikes and lockouts).
Distinguish between fire insurance and life insurance on any three bases.

Nature of risk: fire — uncertain; life — certain (death), only time uncertain.
Compensation: fire — actual loss or sum insured, whichever is less (indemnity); life — fixed sum assured.
Period: fire — usually one year; life — long term.
Insurable interest: fire — at taking the policy and at loss; life — only at taking the policy.
Object: fire — protection; life — protection and investment.
la: Jeevan insured his property with AIG for ₹6 crore and MetLife for ₹4 crore. An earthquake caused damage of ₹3 crore and he claimed ₹3 crore from each insurer. (a) Identify and explain the principle violated. (b) Explain one more principle of insurance.

(a) Contribution (with indemnity). When the same property is insured with more than one insurer, the insurers share the loss in proportion to their policies, and the insured cannot recover more than his actual loss. Jeevan can get only ₹3 crore in all: AIG pays 6/10 × 3 = ₹1.8 crore and MetLife 4/10 × 3 = ₹1.2 crore.
(b) Utmost good faith — both parties must disclose all material facts honestly; hiding them makes the contract void. (Or indemnity, subrogation, insurable interest, mitigation, causa proxima.)
What is insurance? Explain the principles of contribution and mitigation.

Insurance is a contract in which the insurer, for a premium, promises to compensate the insured for loss from specified risks.
Contribution: if the same subject matter is insured with several insurers, the loss is shared by them in proportion to the sums insured; the insured cannot claim the full loss from each.
Mitigation: when a mishap occurs the insured must take all reasonable steps to reduce the loss, acting as if the property were not insured; he cannot be careless because of insurance.
Mohan took a ₹1,00,000 fire policy. Fire caused a loss of ₹30,000, but he claimed the full ₹1,00,000. Name and explain the principle he violated.

Principle of indemnity. Insurance only restores the insured to the position he was in before the loss; he cannot make a profit from it. Compensation is the actual loss or the sum insured, whichever is less, so Mohan gets only ₹30,000.

or: What purpose does marine insurance serve? Explain the types of marine policies useful to exporters and importers.

Marine insurance protects ship-owners and traders against perils of the sea — loss of the ship (hull), the goods (cargo) and the freight.
Policies: (1) time policy — covers a fixed period, usually a year; (2) voyage policy — a particular voyage; (3) mixed policy — a voyage within a fixed time; (4) floating policy — one large sum, reduced as each shipment is declared, useful for regular exporters.

la: What is marine insurance? Explain cargo, hull and freight insurance.

Marine insurance is a contract by which the insurer (underwriter) indemnifies the owner of a ship or cargo against perils of the sea.
Cargo insurance — covers the goods carried against loss by storm, sinking, etc.
Hull insurance — covers the ship itself.
Freight insurance — covers loss of the freight the shipping company would earn if the cargo is lost or damaged.
Explain the principles of indemnity, subrogation and insurable interest.

Indemnity: the insured is compensated only for the actual loss, up to the sum insured; he cannot profit (fire and marine, not life).
Subrogation: after paying the claim the insurer gets the insured's rights in the damaged property.
Insurable interest: the insured must stand to suffer financial loss from the event — in life insurance when taking the policy, in marine at the time of loss, in fire at both times.
